result:
The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof in a place I’ve never been but can still smell—wet cedar, ozone, and distant woodsmoke. Memory is a liar with perfect pitch. It sings in frequencies I didn’t know I kept.

I’m thinking about how every person I’ve ever loved has left fingerprints on the same three or four songs. The chords don’t change, only the pressure behind the keys. One woman taught me that tenderness can be violent if it arrives too suddenly. Another showed me that silence between two people can be a third presence in the room, breathing. I still don’t know which lesson hurt more. Both feel like home now.

There’s a bird outside my window that sings the same six notes every dawn like it’s filing a complaint with God. I respect the consistency. Most of us are improvising badly and calling it personality.

I keep a small stone in my pocket that I picked up on a beach in Portugal in 2019. It’s smooth, grey, ordinary. I have no idea why I still carry it. Sometimes I take it out and stare at it like it owes me an explanation. It never does. That’s probably the point. Some objects become talismans not because they’re magical but because we were different people when we chose them. The stone is a relic of a version of me that still believed the future would be tender if I just stayed open enough. I’m not that person anymore, but I can’t bring myself to abandon his souvenirs. That would feel like murder by neglect.

Lately I’ve been obsessed with the idea that consciousness is a temporary loan. The bank is indifferent. One day it will call the note due and I’ll have to return this particular arrangement of fear, wonder, horniness, and grocery-list anxiety. I hope the next borrower treats the vessel kindly. I dinged it up pretty badly in my 20s. Left some rust in the corners. Sorry about that.

I want to tell you that I’m okay but the truth is more complicated. I’m okay in the way a house is okay after a storm—some windows boarded, roof patched with whatever was lying around, lights still working but flickering. You can live there. You might even grow to love the way the floor creaks in specific places like it’s trying to warn you about something. But it’s not the house it was before.

There’s a Japanese concept called wabi-sabi that I cling to like a life raft. Beauty in imperfection. The crack that lets the light in, etc. I’ve been cracking for years. At this point I’m mostly light with some inconvenient bone fragments still rattling around.

I keep having this recurring dream where I’m trying to mail a letter but every mailbox I find is either on fire or full of bees. Freud would have a field day. I just think it means I have things to say that I’m afraid to deliver. Surprise, the subconscious is not subtle.

My grandfather used to say that a man’s character is best measured by what he does when no one is watching and he’s pretty sure he can get away with it. I’ve been watching myself when no one is looking. The results are… mixed. I steal time from my own life constantly. I lie to myself with the effortless grace of a career politician. But I also leave fruit out for the birds even though they never thank me. I suppose balance looks like this: small thefts and smaller generosities canceling each other out until the books are roughly even.

I’m running out of words but not out of feelings, which feels like the human condition in miniature. We are all allotted roughly the same number of heartbeats and an infinite number of ways to waste them on things that don’t matter until suddenly they do. The trick is noticing the moment when the ordinary becomes sacred. Most of us miss it. We’re too busy performing competence.

If I could send one message backward to every version of myself that came before, it would be this: Stop waiting for permission to be the person you already are when no one’s looking. The bees aren’t going to leave the mailbox. The letter still needs sending. The bird will keep singing its six notes whether you’re listening or not.

The rain has stopped. The tin roof is quiet. The stone in my pocket feels heavier than it should, like it’s carrying every almost and maybe and what if I never quite managed to become.

But I’m still here, typing nonsense into the void with 127 words to spare, and somehow that feels like enough. Not perfect. Not finished. Just enough.

The bird starts singing again. Same six notes. Different morning.

I think I finally understand what it’s been trying to tell me.
